passage: Why are some countries rich and others poor? For several decades the question has been staged as a contest between two answers. One points to geography: to climate, soils, disease and distance from the sea, which shape what can be grown, how healthy workers are and how cheaply goods can be moved. The other points to institutions: to whether property is secure, contracts are enforced and rulers are constrained, which shape whether people find it worth their while to invest, innovate and trade. Each side has its favourite evidence, and each has scored points against the other.

The institutional camp's strongest card is the observation that geography changes slowly while fortunes can change fast. Two halves of a peninsula with the same climate, the same soils and, until the middle of the twentieth century, a shared history can diverge dramatically within a couple of generations once they are placed under different political systems. Institutionalists have also pointed to a pattern among formerly colonised regions: some of those that were relatively densely settled and prosperous five centuries ago are relatively poor today, while some that were thinly populated then are rich now. Geography did not flip in the interval. What changed, the argument goes, were the institutions that colonisers imposed, extractive where there was wealth and labour to seize, more inclusive where settlers came to live.

The geographers' reply is that these comparisons, however striking, do not dispose of their case. A landlocked country far from major markets pays more to export every tonne it produces, whatever its laws say, and a tropical region where malaria is endemic carries a burden of illness that good government can reduce but not abolish overnight. These are direct effects, and no amount of constitutional reform makes a mountain range easier to cross. Geographers add that the peninsula, however vivid, is a single case, and that a single case can show that institutions are capable of mattering without showing how much they usually matter across the wide run of countries.

What both camps tend to overlook is how much of their contest is artificial. The reversal story itself, read carefully, is a story about geography working through institutions. Colonisers chose to settle or to extract partly according to how likely they were to survive the local diseases, and the soils of some regions suited crops that were profitable to grow with coerced labour on large estates. The institutions that resulted were, in this sense, partly geographical in origin, even if they later took on a life of their own. To ask, as statistical exercises often do, how much of the variation in income is due to geography and how much to institutions is to treat as rival causes what are frequently links in a single chain. The exercise can produce a number, but the number answers a question that the history does not pose.

None of this restores geography as destiny. The institutionalists are right that the same land can support very different outcomes, and that a country is not condemned by its latitude. The point is rather that the question 'which matters more?' should give way to the question 'how did they combine here?', which has a different answer in different places and cannot be settled by a single coefficient. For one country the answer may lie largely in a coastline that made trade cheap long before anyone drafted a constitution; for another, in rules imposed by outsiders that outlived the conditions which first made them profitable.

passage: Few claims in social history have travelled as far as the idea that childhood was invented. In its best-known form, put forward in the middle of the twentieth century, it held that medieval Europe had no notion of childhood as a distinct stage of life. Children, on this account, passed almost directly from infancy into the company of adults, working, drinking and dressing as they did; painters showed them as miniature men and women; and parents, facing high infant mortality, refrained from investing much feeling in creatures who might not survive. Childhood as we know it, protected, sentimentalised and set apart, was a discovery of the early modern centuries.

The thesis was a brilliant provocation, and much of it has not survived. Later historians, reading letters, court records, sermons and the evidence of excavated objects, assembled a large body of material showing that medieval parents grieved for dead children, bought or made toys for living ones, and recognised that the young needed particular kinds of care. The argument from paintings proved especially weak. Artistic conventions are not photographs, and an age that painted saints with golden discs around their heads was not simply reporting what it saw. To infer an absence of feeling from an absence of naturalistic portraiture is to mistake a style for a sentiment.

Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that nothing changed. The critics established that medieval people knew children were different and loved them; they did not establish that childhood occupied the same place in social life. What the early modern period did see was the gradual spread of institutions that sorted the young by age and held them apart from adult work: schools divided into classes, a growing literature addressed specifically to children, and eventually laws fixing the ages below which a person could not be employed or married. None of these changes was sudden, and none reached every class or region at once; the children of the poor worked beside adults long after the children of the prosperous had been sent to school. Childhood as a feeling may be ancient. Childhood as a segregated, age-graded stage, organised by institutions, is far more recent.

Seen this way, the original thesis and its critics were partly talking past each other. One side asked whether people recognised and cared for children; the other, without always saying so, asked how societies arranged the passage from birth to adult status. This is why the debate could run for so long without resolution: each side could cite evidence the other did not dispute, because each was answering a different question. The second question is the more fruitful, because it leaves room for the observation that every society has children but not every society has childhood in the same form.

passage: There are two familiar ways of misunderstanding pilgrimage, and they are mirror images of each other. The first treats the journey as mere transport: what matters is arrival at the shrine, the sight of the image or the relic, the bath in the river, and the road is simply the price paid to get there. The second, popular among those who walk old pilgrim routes for reasons they would not call religious, reverses the emphasis. The destination, on this view, is almost a pretext; the real value lies in the walking itself, the days of effort, the strangers met on the way, the slow emptying of the mind.

Each view captures something that pilgrims genuinely report, but both detach two elements that draw their meaning from each other, and neither can be made intelligible without the other. The hardships of the road are not valuable in the abstract. Blistered feet on a hiking holiday are an inconvenience; the same blisters on the way to a sacred place become an offering, a sign of seriousness, a story to be told on return. What converts them is the fixed point towards which they are directed. Equally, the shrine does not possess its full weight for the pilgrim independently of the effort spent reaching it. A visitor who arrives by car on a whim may see exactly what the pilgrim sees and still not have had the pilgrim's experience.

The history of easier travel bears this interdependence out in an unexpected way, and it is worth dwelling on because it runs against a natural expectation. One might have predicted that when roads, railways and buses made distant shrines accessible within hours, the effortful element would simply vanish. In many places it has instead been reintroduced by choice. Pilgrims who have covered most of the distance in comfort often leave the vehicle to walk the final stretch, sometimes barefoot, sometimes on their knees. The effort has been condensed rather than abandoned, as though people sense that arrival without cost would not count as arrival at all.

None of this means that the walker who sets out with no particular reverence is deceived about what he finds. Long days on foot do change people, and the change can be real without being religious. But it is worth noticing what such a walker relinquishes, perhaps without realising it, when the destination becomes optional rather than obligatory. The pilgrim cannot decide halfway that another town would do just as well, and that inability is part of what lends the road its gravity. A journey that could end anywhere is a fine thing; it is simply a different thing from one that must end in a particular place.

passage: Whenever a much-loved novel reaches the screen, a familiar verdict follows: the book was better. Behind the verdict there usually lies a checklist. Was the heroine's age changed, a subplot dropped, a minor character merged with another, the ending softened? Each departure is counted as a fault, and the best adaptation, on this view, is simply the one that departs least, as though the novel were a fixed list of facts and the film an attempt, more or less competent, to copy that list onto a different surface. The habit is understandable, since readers who love a book feel protective of it, but as a standard for judging films it rests on a confusion about what an adaptation is.

A novel and a film do not tell stories in the same way. A novel can spend twenty pages inside a character's head; a film must find something for the camera to look at. A novel handles time loosely, lingering or summarising as it likes, while a film runs at a pace the viewer cannot slow. To reproduce a book's events faithfully is therefore no guarantee of reproducing what the book does. Imagine a novel narrated by a man whose account of himself the reader slowly learns to distrust. A film that simply stages the events he describes, shot plainly and from the outside, may keep every incident and still lose the book entirely, because the book was never really about the incidents but about the gap between what the narrator says and what the reader comes to see.

Conversely, an adaptation that alters a good deal may be truer to its source. A director who invents a visual device to unsettle our trust in what we are shown, framing scenes so that the viewer begins to doubt them, has understood that novel better than one who preserves its plot to the letter. The right question is not how much was kept but whether the film has found its own means of doing what the book did.

None of this means that every liberty is defensible. Some adaptations borrow a famous title for its prestige and its ready-made audience while discarding everything that made the book worth adapting, and the complaint against them is fair. But it is fair for a different reason than the checklist suggests. Such films fail not because they changed things but because they changed the wrong things, keeping the label and throwing away the substance. Fidelity, properly understood, is a matter of purpose rather than of inventory, and judging it requires the critic to say what a book was for before complaining about what a film has left out.

passage: The traditional problem of other minds begins from an asymmetry. I am aware of my own pain directly, the argument runs, but I know of yours only through what you do: the wince, the cry, the hand withdrawn abruptly from the stove. How, then, am I entitled to believe that anything lies behind your behaviour at all? The classic reply is an argument from analogy. In my own case I observe that pain is regularly accompanied by wincing and crying; when I observe wincing and crying in you, I infer that pain is present in you as well, concealed from me but similar to my own.

Critics have long pointed out how fragile this inference is. It generalises from a single case to every other person, which is the kind of reasoning we would reject anywhere else: nobody who had examined one seed from a sack and found it fertile would conclude with any confidence that every seed in the sack would germinate. Worse, the conclusion can never be independently checked. In ordinary induction I can at least test a generalisation against further cases, but I can never step into your experience to confirm that the pain I inferred is really there.

These objections are sound, but they share the assumption they attack: that knowledge of other minds must be an inference from bodily movements to concealed inner states. That assumption does not describe how such knowledge actually arises. A child does not first register a contraction of facial muscles and then hypothesise distress; she sees that her mother is upset, and she sees it as immediately as she sees that the cup is full. Expressions are not evidence from which feelings are deduced. They are, in a great many cases, the very form in which feelings are visible to others, and to treat them as mere outward signs is to describe the face as a mask before asking what lies behind it.

None of this shows that we never reason about other minds. When a stranger's expressions are unfamiliar, when someone is deliberately concealing what she feels, or when we ask whether an octopus or a newborn experiences pain, we do weigh evidence and draw conclusions, and we can be badly wrong. But these are special cases, and they are intelligible only against a background in which most minds are simply seen. The sceptic's mistake is to take the hard case as the model for every case, and then to wonder why the model will not support the confidence we ordinarily have.

passage: Trade statistics were designed for a world in which goods were made in one place and sold in another. A customs officer records the full value of a shipment as it crosses the border and attributes it to the country from which it was sent. When a product is made from start to finish in a single country, this convention is harmless. When it is assembled from parts made in a dozen, the convention produces a curious distortion: the country where the last screw is turned is credited with the entire value of the product, including the much larger share that was created elsewhere and merely passed through.

Consider a hypothetical tablet computer assembled in one country from a display made in a second, chips designed in a third and fabricated in a fourth, and software written in a fifth. When the finished tablet is shipped to a sixth country, the statistics record an export of its full factory price from the assembling country, though the work done there may account for only a small fraction of that price. The bilateral balance between the assembler and the buyer swells accordingly, while the suppliers of the costlier components, whose contribution travels unseen inside the assembler's shipment, appear in the bilateral figures as having sold nothing to the final market at all.

Statisticians have responded by trying to trace value added: to ask, for each product, how much of its value was created in each country, and to tally trade on that basis. The striking feature of the results is not that a country's overall position changes, for it largely does not. Its balance with the world as a whole is much the same however one counts, since the value of each imported component is recorded once as an import and again inside the export, and the two entries cancel. What changes is the map: the bilateral balances that attract political attention are redistributed, often substantially, from assemblers towards the countries that supply the most valuable parts.

This matters because bilateral balances are routinely read as a scorecard of who is gaining at whose expense, and policy is sometimes made on that reading. A tariff aimed at the country with which a large deficit is recorded may, on the value-added view, fall chiefly on workers who contributed a modest share of what was bought, while leaving untouched the countries that contributed the most. The value-added figures are not beyond dispute. They depend on tables of who buys inputs from whom that are compiled infrequently and filled out with estimates, and they cannot replace the gross figures that customs administrations need for their own purposes. But one need not regard them as precise to see that they expose a habit of reading the gross bilateral figures as though they measured something they were never built to measure.

passage: Few political ideals are invoked as often, or defined as loosely, as the rule of law. In one usage it names a set of formal properties of a legal order: laws should be general rather than aimed at particular persons, public rather than secret, prospective rather than retroactive, clear enough to be followed, stable enough to be relied on, and applied by courts that are independent of those who hold power. In another usage the phrase stands for a much larger package. A state governed by the rule of law, on this richer view, is one that also protects fundamental rights, holds free elections and distributes its burdens fairly. Whatever is admirable in a constitutional democracy tends to be gathered under the same heading.

The richer view has an obvious appeal. It seems perverse to praise a legal order for its clarity and consistency while it applies clear and consistent laws that strip a minority of its property or bar it from public life. Yet the inclusive definition carries a cost that its defenders seldom count. If the rule of law means everything good about a political system, the phrase ceases to pick out anything in particular. We lose the ability to say, of one regime, that its laws are cruel but at least public and predictable, or of another that it has excellent statutes on paper which officials ignore whenever it suits them. These are different failings, calling for different remedies, and a vocabulary that cannot separate them is a poorer instrument for judging governments, not a more generous one.

The formal conception, moreover, is not as morally empty as its critics allege. A law that is public and prospective allows people to know in advance what will be required of them and to arrange their lives around it; a law applied by independent courts constrains the officials who administer it as well as the citizens who are subject to it. These are real goods even when the content of the law is objectionable, because they leave the governed some room to anticipate, avoid and contest what is done to them. It is also worth noticing that governments bent on oppression rarely find formal legality congenial. They tend to prefer secret directives, retroactive offences, vague charges that can be stretched to fit any critic, and enforcement that falls on enemies and spares friends. The formal requirements, in other words, get in the way of a great deal of injustice, even if they forbid none of it outright.

This last point should not be pressed too far. The tendency of formality to obstruct oppression is a matter of experience, not of logic, and experience includes regimes that pursued grave injustice through meticulously drafted, publicly promulgated and impartially enforced laws. A defender of the thin conception must concede that legality of this kind is compatible with deep wrong, and that its tendency to discourage abuse is a probability rather than a guarantee. What can be claimed is narrower: that formal legality is one distinct virtue a legal order may have or lack, that its absence makes most other wrongs easier to commit, and that we see it most clearly when we refuse to let it stand for every other virtue at once. Questions about whether the laws are just, whether the rulers were chosen freely and whether the burdens are fairly shared remain, on this view, as urgent as ever; they are simply different questions, and they deserve to be asked in their own terms.

passage: When European travellers and administrators first described marriages in which the groom's family transferred cattle, cloth or other goods to the bride's family, many of them reached for the language of the market. The bride, they concluded, was being bought. The description had the appeal of simplicity, and it fitted a ready-made story in which other peoples' customs were cruder versions of the observers' own commercial habits. Words such as 'price' and 'purchase' entered official reports, and they shaped how the custom was seen long after closer study had cast doubt on them. The description also misread, in nearly every important respect, what the transfer did.

Consider first where the goods go. In many systems they are not kept by the bride's father as profit but are distributed among a wide circle of her kin, each of whom thereby acquires an interest in the marriage succeeding. Consider next where they go afterwards. Often the cattle received when a daughter marries are the very cattle used to secure a wife for her brother, so that a herd travels from family to family and the transfers form a chain linking households that may never meet. A purchase ends a relationship between buyer and seller; this transfer begins several. Consider, finally, what the transfer secures. In a number of societies what passes with the goods is not the woman herself but the affiliation of her future children to the husband's lineage, which is why, in some of them, the goods must be returned if the marriage ends before any children are born.

On this reading, bridewealth is less a price than a contract between groups, and one that gives the bride's family a continuing stake in how she is treated. A family that has shared the goods out among its members, and may have to gather them again in order to return them, has reason both to support the marriage and to intervene when it goes badly. The goods, in other words, work less like a payment than like a pledge, and a pledge held by many hands is harder to ignore than one held by a single man.

It would be naive, however, to treat this as the whole story. Where cash has replaced cattle and the sums demanded have risen with the incomes of urban grooms, the transfer can begin to behave much more like a price: it is negotiated against the bride's education or earning power, it is kept by a narrower set of relatives, and young men may delay marriage for years in order to raise it. Critics who see a market in such arrangements are not simply repeating the old error. The lesson is not that the travellers were wrong and the custom is innocent, but that the meaning of a transfer depends on the web of obligations around it, and that when the web thins, the meaning changes.

passage: Most people in the modern West assume that a name is a fixed possession, given once at birth and carried, with perhaps one change at marriage, until death. The assumption is so deep that we rarely notice it is an assumption at all, yet in a wide range of societies a person's name has been expected to change over a lifetime, and one of the commonest occasions for the change is the birth of a child. When a man becomes known as the father of his first child, or a woman as the mother of hers, anthropologists speak of teknonymy: naming a parent through the offspring. The Arabic custom of addressing a man as Abu, 'father of', followed by the name of his eldest son, is perhaps the most familiar instance, but the practice in various forms has been recorded on several continents.

It is tempting to read teknonymy as a simple sign that children are prized, and there is something in this. But the more interesting point is what the custom reveals about how such societies understand a person. In a system of fixed names, identity is treated as something an individual owns from the start, and relationships are added to it later, like rooms built onto a house. In a teknonymous system the order is reversed: a person becomes fully visible in social life only by standing in a relationship; the new name announces not that the individual has changed but that their position in a web of kin has changed. One is addressed less as a self than as a point where generations meet.

This also explains a feature that puzzles outsiders. In some communities it becomes mildly rude to use the old personal name of an adult who has a child, much as it would be odd for us to call a judge by a childhood nickname in court. The personal name has not been forbidden; it has simply been outranked by a title that carries more social information. Where the practice extends further, so that a grandparent is named after a grandchild, a person's name can track their rise through the generations, and the most senior people come to be known almost entirely through their descendants.

None of this should be romanticised, for a system that names people through their children can be hard on those who have none, who may remain, in the language of address, permanently junior. Nor is the Western fixed name as individualistic as it looks, since a surname itself announces a lineage. The contrast is one of emphasis rather than of kind, but the emphasis matters. To change a person's name at the birth of a child is to state, every time that person is greeted, that adulthood is not a private achievement but a place in a sequence.

passage: Few observations seem less in need of explanation than the darkness of the night sky. The sun sets and the heavens go dark; what else would they do? Yet for several centuries astronomers who took seriously the idea of an infinite, unchanging cosmos found that darkness genuinely puzzling, and their reasoning deserves to be reconstructed, because its premises once seemed almost beyond question. Suppose that stars are scattered more or less uniformly through boundless space. Then any direction in which an observer looks, pursued far enough, must sooner or later meet the bright disc of a star. Remote stars certainly look dimmer than nearby ones, but the number of stars at each successive distance grows in step with the dimming, so that every shell of space contributes as much light as the one inside it. On these assumptions the heavens should glow in all directions with the brilliance of the solar surface.

The first replies tried to rescue the infinite universe by blocking the light. Perhaps clouds of dust between the stars absorbed the glow of the most distant ones. The suggestion sounds reasonable until one follows it through, for dust that absorbs light for long enough is warmed by it, and eventually it glows as brightly as the light it swallows. Over an unlimited span of time, absorption delays the problem; it does not remove it. Other proposals arranged the stars in clusters within clusters, so that lines of sight could slip between them, but these seemed contrived, a geometry invented to answer a single awkward question.

The resolution now accepted is both simpler and stranger. The universe we can observe has a finite age, and light, however swift, needs time to cross space. Most directions therefore never terminate on a star, because the glow of sufficiently remote stars is still in transit, and to look far enough out is to look back to an epoch before any stars had formed. The expansion of space contributes a second effect, stretching the light of faraway sources to longer and feebler wavelengths. Neither point needs to be accepted merely because it dissolves the paradox; each is supported by independent lines of evidence gathered long after the puzzle was first posed.

It would be an exaggeration to say that the darkness of the night proves that the universe had a beginning. Taken alone, it rules out only one combination of assumptions, namely that space is infinite, evenly stocked with stars and unchanging forever, but that is no small thing. A fact available to anyone who steps outside after sunset turns out to be incompatible with what was, for a long time, the most natural picture of the cosmos. The lesson is less about stars than about observation, for the most ordinary features of experience are not always the least informative; sometimes they seem ordinary only because we have stopped asking why they are as they are.

passage: Anthropologists have long described rites of passage as moving in three phases. The person undergoing the rite is first separated from an existing status, then passes through a transitional period in which he or she belongs to neither the old condition nor the new, and is finally incorporated into the community in a new role: adult, married, initiated, ordained. Of these phases the middle one, often called liminal, from the Latin word for a threshold, has attracted by far the most attention, and for good reason. It is there that most of the strange features of such rites are concentrated: seclusion in the forest or a special hut, the shaving of heads, the wearing of identical plain garments, the suspension of names, the imposition of hardship and silence.

A simple reading treats these features as a waiting room, a pause while the real change, the conferral of new status, is prepared offstage. This misses their function. Stripping novices of names, clothing and possessions removes the markers by which they were previously ranked, so that for a time sons of important families and sons of poor ones are indistinguishable. Shared hardship then does two things at once. It makes the novices receptive to instruction, since people deprived of their usual footing listen differently, and it binds them to one another in a way that often outlasts the ritual, creating cohorts whose loyalty cuts across lineage and wealth.

In recent decades, however, the idea has travelled far from its origins, and something has been lost on the way. The liminal phase is now often celebrated as a zone of freedom, creativity and play, and the word is applied to almost any in-between experience: the years after school, a period of unemployment, a long journey abroad. This enthusiasm overlooks how tightly the traditional threshold was managed. Elders set its length, prescribed what novices could eat and say, and decided when it was over. Its ambiguity was real, but it was ambiguity held inside a firm frame, and its whole point was the return.

That frame is what most modern transitions lack. A young person who drifts between education and employment may experience the disorientation of the threshold without its discipline, its companions or, above all, its exit. There is no moment at which the community declares the passage complete and receives the person in a new capacity. None of this implies that the old rites should be revived, since their authority rested on forms of social life that no longer exist. But the comparison suggests that what made liminality productive was not the openness that its modern admirers praise. It was the certainty that the openness would end.

passage: In 1865 the economist William Stanley Jevons argued that Britain's growing skill at burning coal efficiently would not conserve its coal but hasten its exhaustion. Cheaper steam power, he reasoned, would make steam worth using in trades that had never used it, and the extra demand would more than swallow the saving. The idea has enjoyed a curious afterlife in contemporary environmental argument. It is invoked today, often with a note of triumph, by those who doubt that better lamps, engines and insulation can do much for the climate. It is dismissed, often with equal confidence, by those who regard efficiency as the cheapest source of clean energy there is. Both camps tend to treat the question as if it had a single answer, when the size of the effect plainly depends on circumstances.

The mechanism itself is not in dispute. When a service becomes cheaper to provide, people generally consume more of it, and the additional consumption offsets part of the anticipated reduction. A household that insulates its walls may heat more rooms, or keep them warmer; a driver whose car burns less fuel per kilometre may drive further, or buy a heavier car next time. Economists call the part of the expected saving that is eaten up in this way the rebound. What is disputed is its size. Where demand for a service is already close to saturation, as with lighting in a well-lit home, the rebound tends to be modest: few people want their rooms twice as bright merely because brightness has become cheap. Where energy is a basic input to production, and cheaper energy lets whole industries expand, the rebound can be large, and in the case Jevons studied it may well have exceeded the saving.

There is also a subtler and less visible channel of transmission. Money saved on fuel does not vanish; it is spent on something else, and that something else uses energy too. A family that spends less on petrol may take a holiday flight it could not previously afford. These indirect effects are considerably harder to trace than the direct ones, which is one reason why published estimates of the total rebound vary so widely across studies and sectors.

The sensible conclusion is neither that efficiency is futile nor that it is sufficient. Efficiency genuinely improves people's material circumstances: they obtain more warmth, light and travel for their money, and that is a gain in its own right. But if the aim is to reduce total energy use or emissions, efficiency works best when it is paired with something that keeps energy costly enough that the saving is not simply spent on using more of it, such as a tax on carbon or a cap on emissions. Efficiency then supplies the comfort, and the price makes sure that the comfort is not bought with the very fuel that was meant to be saved.

passage: Anyone who watches visitors in a busy gallery will notice how briefly most pictures are looked at. A few seconds for the image, a little longer for the label, and the visitor moves on. In response, many museums now promote what is sometimes called slow looking: sessions in which participants are invited to sit before a single work for a quarter of an hour or more, noting whatever comes to their attention. The premise is simple and attractive. We miss what is in paintings because we do not give them time, and if we gave them time, they would show us more.

The practice has real merits, and its critics should concede them. It interrupts the habit, encouraged by crowded rooms and handheld screens, of treating a picture as something to be recognised and ticked off. It gives permission to stay, which many visitors seem to need. And it does sometimes yield discoveries: a figure in the background that had gone unnoticed, a repeated colour that ties distant parts of the canvas together. But the premise behind it, that duration by itself turns into perception, is weaker than it looks. Fifteen minutes in front of a canvas can be fifteen minutes of reverie, of thinking about lunch, or of staring with growing unease at a surface that refuses to become interesting. Time is a condition of seeing, not a cause of it.

What turns time into seeing is a question. The art historian who notices in a moment that the light in a landscape falls from two directions does not see faster because her eyes are better; she sees because she has learned to ask where the light comes from, and the painting answers. Expertise, in this sense, is a stock of questions that direct the eye, questions that are not mysterious endowments but are acquired, often laboriously, through the comparison of many works, and that can therefore in principle be taught. This explains why experts often see in seconds what a patient beginner misses in an hour. The beginner is not looking less; he is looking without a question, and an unguided gaze tends to settle on whatever is largest, brightest or most familiar.

Yet the expert's advantage carries a risk of its own, and here the advocates of slow looking have a point that their own premise obscures. A stock of questions is also a stock of expectations. The historian who knows what to look for in a painting of a certain school may stop looking once she has found it, filing the picture under its category and failing to notice what does not fit. Questions direct the eye, but they also tell it where it need not go. Some of the most valuable observations a viewer can make come from setting expertise aside long enough to be surprised, and slow looking at its best is precisely a technique for producing that suspension.

The two halves of the matter therefore need each other. Time without questions drifts; questions without time confirm what they expected. Neither ingredient is dispensable, and neither, taken in isolation, is sufficient for the kind of perception that the advocates of slow looking rightly prize. The most useful practice is neither the patient blankness that slow looking sometimes encourages nor the quick classification that expertise permits, but an alternation between them: a period of asking, a period of letting the asking lapse, and a return to the picture to see whether it has said something the questions did not predict.

passage: A common complaint about relative poverty lines is that they confuse poverty with inequality. If a household counts as poor whenever its income falls below, say, half of the median, then a country in which everyone became twice as rich would have exactly as many poor people as before. Critics take this as a decisive objection: a measure that cannot register a general rise in living standards, they say, is measuring the spread of incomes and calling it hardship. The objection is tidy, and it is not wrong about the arithmetic. It is wrong, I think, about what poverty is.

Being poor has never meant only lacking the calories and shelter needed to stay alive. It has meant being unable to do what one's neighbours take for granted: to send a child to school in clothes that will not draw mockery, to return a dinner invitation, to keep a telephone so that an employer can call. These requirements are set by the society one lives in, and they rise as that society grows richer. A family that could once manage without a refrigerator or a bank account cannot easily do so when shops, schools and employers assume that it has both. Relative lines track this moving threshold of participation, and that is exactly why their indifference to a uniform rise in incomes is not a defect. If everyone's income doubled, the cost of taking part in ordinary life would roughly double too.

This does not mean that relative measures can stand alone. Their weakness shows most plainly in a recession. When median income falls, the line falls with it, and a household whose income has not changed may be counted as having escaped poverty while its circumstances are no better, and its anxieties perhaps worse. A measure that reports falling poverty in the middle of a slump will strike most people as perverse, and they will be right. Absolute lines, fixed in real terms at some past standard, have the opposite virtue: they register whether the poorest are gaining or losing ground in purchasing power, whatever is happening to everyone else.

The sensible conclusion is not to choose between the two but to read them together, as answers to different questions. An absolute line asks whether the poor can buy more than they could before; a relative line asks whether they can still live as members of the society around them. A government that improves the first while the second worsens has achieved something real, but it has not abolished poverty, and it should not be allowed to claim that it has.

passage: When a population of elephants recovers, the news is usually reported as a conservation triumph, and in an important sense it is one. But the recovery is experienced very differently at the edge of the forest. For a farming household whose maize or paddy lies along an elephant's route, a single night's visit can destroy a season's income, and the danger is not only to crops: people walking home after dark, or guarding fields from makeshift platforms, are injured and sometimes killed. The benefits of a thriving elephant population are spread thinly across a nation, or across the world; its costs are concentrated on a few villages.

Discussions of the problem often frame it as one of attitudes. Farmers who retaliate, it is said, need to be taught to value wildlife, and coexistence is presented as a disposition that can be cultivated through awareness campaigns. There is something to this, since tolerance of wild animals varies a great deal between communities and is shaped by tradition as well as by loss. Yet to treat hostility as ignorance is to misread it. A farmer who has lost three harvests to elephants may understand their ecological importance perfectly well and still be unable to afford them.

The more honest framing is distributive. Coexistence is not a state of mind but an arrangement about who bears which costs. Compensation schemes acknowledge this in principle, but in practice they are often slow, demand paperwork that poor households struggle to complete, and pay for the market value of a damaged crop while ignoring the sleepless nights, the children kept from school to guard fields and the fear that hangs over every harvest. A scheme that pays a fraction of the loss, a year late, does not shift the burden; it documents it.

Practical deterrents have their place. Some communities have experimented with fences hung with beehives, which elephants tend to avoid, or with repellents made from chilli and with networks that warn villages of approaching herds, and where these work they reduce losses at modest cost. But deterrents move the problem as often as they solve it, pushing elephants onto the next village's fields. The underlying question remains political: whether the wider society that values elephants is willing to pay, promptly and in full, those who live beside them. Until it is, appeals for tolerance ask the poorest people in the landscape to subsidise everyone else's enjoyment of a recovered species.

passage: For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, scholars who wrote about the history of writing liked to arrange the world's scripts on a ladder. At the bottom stood picture-writing, in which signs resembled the things they named; above it came scripts in which signs stood for whole words; above those, scripts whose signs stood for syllables; and at the summit, the alphabet, in which a few dozen letters represented the individual sounds of speech. The ladder told a story of progress toward economy and abstraction, and it rarely escaped notice that the peoples occupying the topmost rung were, in most such accounts, the authors' own.

The ladder has not survived scrutiny well. Its first difficulty is descriptive. The scripts it consigned to the lower rungs were seldom what it said they were: the characters of Chinese, often presented as pictures of things, are in large part compounds in which one component indicates meaning and another indicates, however loosely, sound. Such a script is not a halting step toward phonetic writing but a different and highly developed answer to the problem of recording a language. Its second difficulty is historical. The sequence it describes is, at best, the history of one lineage of scripts in one region, and to present it as the path that all writing must follow is to mistake a family tree for a law of nature.

The deeper difficulty concerns the standard of judgment. The ladder assumed that a script should be ranked by how few signs it needs, so that fewer signs meant a better system. Economy of inventory is a real virtue; a child learning an alphabet with regular spelling can sound out unfamiliar words within a few years, and few would deny that this is an advantage. But it is one criterion among several. A script that represents meaning directly can be read across spoken varieties that differ so much in pronunciation that their speakers cannot follow one another in conversation. A mixed system, such as the one used for Japanese, can show at a glance which parts of a sentence carry lexical content and which carry grammar, an aid to rapid reading once the system is mastered. And an alphabet is only as economical as its spelling permits; a language whose spelling has drifted far from its pronunciation, as English has, can oblige its learners to memorise many words almost as wholes.

None of this implies that scripts are equal in every respect or that the choice of script is unimportant. The costs of learning differ, and some of them fall heavily on those with the least schooling. A script deliberately devised in fifteenth-century Korea, whose letter shapes reflect how the sounds they represent are produced, was designed with exactly such learners in mind, and its designers evidently believed that some ways of writing were better than others for certain ends. That belief is a ranking of a kind, but it is a ranking relative to a purpose, which is precisely what the ladder lacked.

It is also worth noticing what the ladder's critics should not claim. To deny that the alphabet is the summit of writing is not to say that literacy rates owe nothing to scripts; they plainly owe something. It is to say that they owe much more to schools, to the availability of reading matter and to whether reading pays, and that societies with very different scripts have reached near-universal literacy once those conditions were in place. The ladder told us that the script was destiny. The record suggests it is closer to terrain: it shapes the route, but it does not decide who arrives.

passage: Virtue ethics asks not what rule an action follows or what outcome it produces but what kind of person performs it. Its central concepts are traits of character such as honesty, courage and compassion, conceived as stable dispositions that lead a person to act well across a wide range of circumstances. The compassionate person does not help only when it is convenient or when someone is watching; her compassion shows itself in the market and at home, towards friends and towards strangers. It is this breadth that distinguishes a virtue from a habit, and it is what makes the attribution of a virtue a substantial claim about a person rather than a summary of what she happened to do last week.

In recent decades a group of critics, often called situationists, has argued that this picture is empirically naive. They point to a body of experimental work in social psychology, some of it now disputed, which has been taken to show that small and morally irrelevant features of a situation, such as whether a person is in a hurry or in a pleasant mood, predict whether she will help someone in need far better than anything we know about her character. If behaviour is driven so heavily by circumstance, the critics conclude, then broad traits of the kind virtue ethics requires are rare or nonexistent, and a theory built around them describes a psychology that human beings do not have. On this view, to call someone honest or kind is less a discovery about her than a story we tell to make her conduct look more orderly than it is.

The argument is more damaging to some versions of virtue ethics than to others. If the theory claimed that most people possess the virtues, the evidence would tell heavily against it. But the classical tradition never claimed this. It held that full virtue is difficult, uncommon and achieved, if at all, through long training, and that most people are a mixture of good impulses and weak resolve. Evidence that ordinary people are easily swayed by circumstance is exactly what such a tradition would predict. Indeed, much of the advice it offers, to avoid temptations rather than trust oneself to resist them and to choose one's companions with care, makes sense only on the assumption that character is fragile.

This reply, however, has a cost that its defenders do not always acknowledge. If genuine virtue is so rare that experimental samples almost never contain it, then virtue ethics can no longer claim the advantage it has often advertised over its rivals: that it describes moral life as it is actually lived, in terms of real people and their recognisable qualities. An ideal that almost no one embodies may still be worth pursuing, but it begins to look less like a description of character and more like a rule of the kind the theory set out to replace, a standard against which conduct is measured rather than a source from which it flows.

The situationist challenge, then, does not refute virtue ethics, but it changes what the theory can coherently promise. The theory can keep its account of the ideal, or its claim to realism about ordinary people, but it is hard to see how it can keep both. Which it should give up is a question that experiments alone cannot answer, since it depends on what we want an ethical theory to do: to guide those who aspire to goodness, or to describe those whose characters are already formed.

passage: The replacement of the scroll by the codex is one of the quiet revolutions in the history of reading. In the Mediterranean world of the early centuries of the common era, a book was usually a long roll of papyrus, wound on itself and read by unrolling one column at a time; within a few hundred years the dominant form had become the codex, a stack of folded sheets bound along one edge, which remains the shape of most books today. The customary explanation for the change is economy: a codex uses both sides of its writing material, it packs more text into less volume, and it is easier to carry. All of this is true, and none of it is quite enough.

The economic story struggles with timing. If thrift alone had driven the change, one would expect the codex to have spread fastest where writing material was scarce and to have triumphed as soon as its savings were obvious. Instead it lingered for generations as a humble format for notebooks, accounts and school exercises, while prestigious literature stayed on the roll. Its adoption was uneven in ways that cost does not explain; some communities, early Christian ones among them, seem to have taken it up well before their neighbours, for reasons that probably had as much to do with identity and use as with price.

A more illuminating difference lies in how the two forms allow a reader to move through a text. A scroll is constructed for continuous reading from beginning to end: to find a passage near the middle, one must wind through everything that precedes it, and comparing two distant passages is awkward enough that readers leaned heavily on memory instead. A codex, by contrast, can be opened anywhere. A finger can hold one place while the eye checks another; a page can be marked, numbered and returned to. The codex, in other words, made the text navigable, and navigation changed what reading could be. A legal compilation, a book of scripture to be cited in argument, a technical manual to be consulted rather than recited: these are works one enters at a point rather than travels through, and they suit the codex far better than the roll.

It would be a mistake to convert this into a narrative of inevitable progress. Readers of rolls were not deprived; they cultivated habits of memorisation and recitation that served their purposes admirably, and something of that intimacy with a whole text may have been lost when books became places in which to look things up. Nor did the codex create consultative reading out of nothing. But the form encouraged certain practices and discouraged others, and over centuries the encouragement told. The later apparatus of the book, page numbers, tables of contents and indexes, would have been nearly pointless on a roll. It is the codex's logic worked out in full.

passage: Discussions of population ageing tend to begin with a single number. The old-age dependency ratio divides the number of people above a fixed age, usually sixty-five, by the number of people of working age, conventionally fifteen to sixty-four. As birth rates fall and lives lengthen the ratio rises, and a rising ratio is read as a growing burden: fewer shoulders, it is said, bearing the weight of more pensioners. The image is vivid and the arithmetic is simple, which is precisely why the measure deserves more suspicion than it usually receives.

The ratio rests on two equations that are rarely stated. The first is that everyone between fifteen and sixty-four supports others and everyone above sixty-five is supported by them. Neither half is true. Large numbers of people of working age are in education, unemployed, caring full-time for relatives or otherwise outside paid work, while many people beyond the threshold continue to earn, to pay taxes and, perhaps most importantly, to provide unpaid care. In many families it is grandparents whose looking after small children allows both parents to hold jobs; on the ratio's accounting, those grandparents appear only as a cost. The same error runs in the other direction for the many people in their fifties who have left paid work early through illness or redundancy, and who depend on others well before the line is reached.

The second equation is that a given age means the same thing in every generation. A sixty-five-year-old today in most countries can expect to live considerably longer, and in better health, than a sixty-five-year-old of the generation in which the threshold was fixed. To keep the line at sixty-five as life expectancy rises is to classify as old an ever larger share of people who are, by the standards that originally justified the line, not old at all. Some demographers have proposed measuring age prospectively, by the years a person can expect still to live rather than the years already lived; on such measures, populations age considerably more slowly than the headline ratio suggests.

None of this means that ageing is costless. The final years of a long life often bring a need for intensive medical and personal care, and as more people reach advanced old age that need grows in ways no redefinition can wish away. The objection is not to concern but to calibration. A measure that counts heads by birthday rather than activity by circumstance will tend to exaggerate the problem in its general form and to obscure it in the specific form, very late life, in which it is most acute.

passage: It is often said that explaining a joke kills it, and anyone who has tried to rescue a failed pun by spelling out its double meaning knows that the saying is true as far as it goes. The listener nods, perhaps smiles politely, but the laugh that should have come does not. The usual inference drawn from this experience is that humour is a fragile, almost mystical thing, which analysis can only damage, and that the serious study of comedy is a contradiction in terms. The experience is real; the inference does not follow from it.

Consider why the explanation fails. A joke typically sets up one way of understanding a situation and then, in a single move, reveals that a second way was available all along. The pleasure lies largely in the listener's own discovery of the second meaning, in the sudden reorganisation that happens in his head rather than on the page. Explanation takes this work away from him. It hands over the result without the leap, much as being told the answer to a riddle deprives one of the satisfaction of solving it. The joke is not killed because it has been examined; it is killed because the examination has been done for the listener, before he could do it himself, at the very moment that was meant to be his.

Seen in this way, the failure of explained jokes tells us something about humour, namely that it depends on an active contribution from the audience, and this is exactly the kind of thing analysis can discover. There is nothing self-defeating in studying how jokes work, any more than there is in studying how riddles work. The student of comedy who analyses a routine afterwards does not expect to laugh at the analysis; he expects to understand the laugh he has already had. The two activities are simply different, and the second does not undo the first.

There is even a case for explanation in the moment, under certain conditions. A joke that turns on an unfamiliar word, a local custom or an allusion to a book the listener has not read cannot produce its leap, because one of the two meanings is not available to him at all. Here a brief explanation does not perform the leap on the listener's behalf; it only supplies the missing ground from which he can make it, and a listener who has been told what the allusion refers to will sometimes laugh a moment later, on his own. The skilled explainer, like the skilled comedian, knows how much to say and when to stop.
